ety.text: From Middle English but, buten, boute, bouten, from Old English būtan (“without, outside of, except, only”), from Proto-West Germanic *biūtan, *biūtini, equivalent to be- + out. Compare bin, about.

senses.d: Outside of.

senses.d: Used to repeat an adverb for emphasis; simply; just; absolutely.

senses.d: However, although, nevertheless, on the other hand (introducing a clause contrary to prior belief or in contrast with the preceding clause or sentence).
ex: She is very old but still attractive.

senses.d: On the contrary, rather (as a regular adversative conjunction, introducing a word or clause in contrast or contradiction with the preceding negative clause or sentence).

senses.d: Used at the beginning of a sentence to express opposition to a remark.

senses.d: Except that (introducing a subordinate clause which qualifies a negative statement); also, (archaic) with omission of the subject of the subordinate clause, acting as a negative relative, "except one that", "except such that".

senses.d: Used to link an interjection to the following remark as an intensifier.

senses.d: Without it also being the case that; unless that (introducing a necessary concomitant).
